summary: Finland is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. The land border with Russia is closed, and Russian citizens on Schengen tourist visas are refused entry.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 listing the third countries whose nationals must hold a visa — EUR-Lex
source.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2018/1806, Article 4(1) — stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.

source.name: Visa Code (Regulation (EC) No 810/2009), consolidated text — EUR-Lex
source.instrument: Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas, Article 16(1) (visa fee) and Article 1(1) (stays not exceeding 90 days in any 180-day period), consolidated to 11 June 2024

fee.notes: Issued mainly alongside residence-permit decisions for workers, students, researchers and their families. Most stays over 90 days are handled as residence permits through the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri). Confirm current conditions with the Finnish mission.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland — visas and entry

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland — visas and entry

proofOfFunds.text: Finland’s guideline is roughly €30 per person per day for the stay; border officers assess sufficiency case by case alongside accommodation and tickets. Confirm the current guideline with the Finnish mission.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland — visas and entry

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted virtually everywhere in Finland, including buses, kiosks and market stalls. Many places are card-only, and cash is rarely needed.

safety.text: Finland consistently ranks among the safest countries in the world, with very low crime. The main risks are environmental: severe winter cold in Lapland and slippery pavements in the cities.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Finland travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: June–August offers the midnight sun, lakeside cottages and warm city terraces; December–March is the season for Lapland, husky safaris and the northern lights.

idp.text: Finland is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Finland is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Finland yet.

tips.text: Finland’s eastern land border crossings with Russia are closed until further notice, and Russian citizens traveling on Schengen tourist visas are refused entry — do not plan any overland routing between Finland and Russia.

Non-EU visitors are registered biometrically in the EU Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorization is being phased in for visa-exempt travelers. Check the official EU site before you fly.
For Lapland in winter, pack for -20°C or colder — layered thermal clothing, insulated boots and a proper hat; tour operators often lend thermal suits, but everyday gear is your own responsibility.
Do not bother exchanging much cash — Finland is close to cashless, and some cafés and buses accept cards or mobile payments only.
Finland connects seamlessly with Sweden, Norway and Estonia. All Schengen, so there are no border checks but your 90/180-day allowance is shared across the whole area.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Finland?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90), applied for through Finland’s missions or visa centers.

faq.question: Does time in Finland count against my Schengen 90-day limit?
faq.answer: Yes. Finland is fully in the Schengen Area, so days spent there count toward the single 90-days-in-180 allowance shared with all other Schengen countries, including Sweden, Norway and Estonia.

faq.question: Can I cross between Finland and Russia by land?
faq.answer: No — Finland has closed its eastern land border crossings with Russia until further notice, and Russian citizens holding Schengen visas issued for tourism are refused entry. Only narrow exemptions such as family, work and humanitarian grounds apply.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Finland?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travelers will need the €20 online authorization before traveling to Finland and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU ETIAS site for the current status.

faq.question: When can I see the northern lights in Finland?
faq.answer: The aurora season in Finnish Lapland runs roughly from late August to April, with the best odds on clear, dark nights between December and March away from city lights. No special permits are needed, just warm clothing.
